title: Formal analysis of an artwork
examples: How do I talk about the line work in a painting?
What is the difference between describing and interpreting?
Can you give me an example of analyzing composition?

explain.say: Today we will look at formal analysis of art.
First we look at line. Line describes the path of a moving point.

draw.text: Line: Path of a moving point

explain.say: Next we look at colour. Colour refers to the hue and intensity used.

items: Hue: Name of the colour (red, blue)

explain.say: Composition is how all the parts are arranged in the artwork.

items: Focal Point: Area of main interest

explain.say: Scale describes the size relationship between objects in the art.
When we describe, we state what we see. For example, the lines are jagged.

faq.q: What is the difference between describing and interpreting?
faq.a: Describing means stating the observable facts about the artwork. Interpreting means suggesting what those facts mean.
asks: How do I know when I am describing?

faq.q: Should I use art vocabulary when I analyze?
faq.a: Yes, using terms like 'hue', 'rhythm', and 'composition' makes your analysis sound informed. It shows you know the concepts.
asks: What are some good art words to use?
Do I need to sound academic?

faq.q: How do I talk about scale effectively?
faq.a: You can compare the object's size to the human body or to other objects in the scene. This helps the reader visualize the difference.
asks: Is scale the same as proportion?
When is scale important to mention?

faq.q: If the composition is chaotic, what should I say?
faq.a: You can describe it as asymmetrical or dynamic. You can interpret that it creates a feeling of energy or tension.
asks: What if the art doesn't look balanced?
Can I say the composition is messy?

faq.q: Do I need to cover all the elements?
faq.a: No, you should focus on the most dominant or important elements. Pick three or four strong points to discuss deeply.
asks: Is it bad if I skip discussing texture?
How many elements should I mention?

facts: Line can be used to suggest movement or direction within a piece.
Colour theory discusses how colours interact to create mood.
Composition refers to the organization of visual elements within the frame.
Scale relates to the perceived size of a subject compared to others.

quiz.say: The way the artist arranges figures to draw the eye across the canvas is an analysis of:
quiz.why: Composition specifically deals with the organization and placement of all elements.

wrong.0: Colour describes the pigment, not how the pigments are placed together.
wrong.1: Scale only compares the size of one thing to another, not the whole layout.
wrong.3: Line is only the path of a single point, not the overall arrangement.

quiz.say: If a statue appears much larger than a person standing next to it, you are analyzing the:
quiz.why: Scale directly addresses the size relationship between objects shown in the artwork.

wrong.0: Composition is about arrangement, not the actual size difference shown.
wrong.1: Colour is about light and pigment, not physical size.
wrong.3: Line describes the edges, not the overall size difference.

quiz.say: When you say 'The cool blues contrast sharply with the warm oranges,' you are analyzing:
quiz.why: This statement specifically discusses the interaction between different hues and temperatures of colour.

wrong.1: Composition is about placement, not the specific relationship between two colours.
wrong.2: Line is a single mark; this statement involves two distinct colour areas.
wrong.3: Scale measures size, which is not what the contrast between blues and oranges describes.
